title: Cardiothoracic ratio
text: The cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) is the maximal horizontal cardiac diameter divided by the maximal internal thoracic diameter on a frontal chest radiograph. On a well-inspired PA film a CTR above 0.50 is conventionally taken as cardiac enlargement. AP and supine projections magnify the heart, so the 0.50 rule over-calls enlargement on them.
source: Danzer CS. The cardiothoracic ratio: an index of cardiac enlargement. Am J Med Sci 1919; Radiopaedia: Cardiothoracic ratio

title: Causes of an enlarged cardiac silhouette
text: An enlarged cardiac silhouette may reflect true chamber enlargement (cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, chronic hypertension), pericardial effusion, or extracardiac factors such as a prominent pericardial fat pad, poor inspiration or rotation. The radiograph cannot separate these; echocardiography is the usual next step.
source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria: Chronic Chest Pain / Dyspnea (Cardiac Origin); Radiopaedia: Cardiomegaly

title: Acting on an enlarged heart
text: A new finding of cardiomegaly should be correlated with symptoms of heart failure, blood pressure history and ECG. Signs of decompensation on the same film - upper lobe venous diversion, interstitial or alveolar oedema, pleural effusions - raise urgency.
source: ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure, 2021

title: Radiographic signs of pleural effusion
text: On an erect frontal radiograph pleural fluid collects first in the posterior and lateral costophrenic recesses. Blunting of the lateral costophrenic angle usually needs roughly 200 to 300 ml of fluid; larger effusions form a meniscus that climbs the lateral chest wall and obscure the hemidiaphragm. Lateral decubitus films and ultrasound detect much smaller volumes.
source: Blackmore CC et al. Assessment of volume of pleural effusion. Radiology 1996; BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease 2023

title: Effusion mimics
text: Pleural thickening, a raised hemidiaphragm, subpulmonic effusion and lower lobe collapse or consolidation can mimic or mask an effusion on a frontal film. Ultrasound is recommended to confirm and to guide any pleural procedure.
source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease 2023

title: Next steps for a new effusion
text: A unilateral effusion without an obvious cause usually warrants ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration for protein, LDH, pH, cytology and microbiology. Bilateral effusions with cardiomegaly most often reflect heart failure and may be managed by treating the cause first.
source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease 2023

title: Recognising a pneumothorax
text: The key sign is a visible visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it, usually at the apex on an erect film. On supine films air rises anteriorly and may show only as a deep sulcus sign or unusual lucency at the lung base. Skin folds, clothing and bullae are common mimics.
source: MacDuff A et al. Management of spontaneous pneumothorax: BTS guideline 2010; Radiopaedia: Pneumothorax

title: Urgency of a pneumothorax
text: A pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise, tracheal or mediastinal shift is a tension pneumothorax and needs immediate decompression on clinical grounds, not after imaging. A stable patient's management depends on symptoms and size; BTS 2023 guidance supports conservative or ambulatory management for selected patients.
source: BTS Guideline for Pleural Disease 2023 (pneumothorax section)

title: Consolidation on chest radiograph
text: Consolidation is lung whose alveolar air has been replaced by fluid, pus, blood, cells or protein. It appears as a confluent opacity that obscures vessels, may show air bronchograms, and silhouettes adjacent borders: loss of the right heart border places it in the right middle lobe, loss of a hemidiaphragm in a lower lobe.
source: Hansell DM et al. Fleischner Society: Glossary of terms for thoracic imaging. Radiology 2008

title: Consolidation and pneumonia
text: In a patient with fever, cough and raised inflammatory markers, new consolidation supports community-acquired pneumonia. Severity is assessed clinically, for example with CURB-65. Radiographic resolution lags clinical recovery by weeks; a follow-up film around six weeks is advised for patients over 50 or smokers to exclude an underlying lesion.
source: NICE guideline NG138 / CG191: Pneumonia in adults; BTS community-acquired pneumonia guideline

title: Differential of airspace opacity
text: Airspace opacity is non-specific. Pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage, aspiration, organising pneumonia and adenocarcinoma can all appear identical to infective consolidation. Distribution, time course and clinical context guide interpretation.
source: Hansell DM et al. Fleischner Society Glossary. Radiology 2008

title: Pulmonary nodule
text: A pulmonary nodule is a rounded opacity up to 30 mm in diameter, surrounded by lung. Larger lesions are masses. Many nodules seen on radiographs are mimics: nipple shadows, rib fractures or calcified costal cartilage, skin lesions and vessels seen end-on.
source: Hansell DM et al. Fleischner Society Glossary. Radiology 2008

title: Following up an incidental nodule
text: A nodule suspected on radiograph is normally characterised with CT. For incidentally found solid nodules on CT the Fleischner Society 2017 guidance bases follow-up on size and risk: under 6 mm usually needs no routine follow-up in low-risk patients, 6 to 8 mm is followed at 6 to 12 months, and over 8 mm is considered for CT at 3 months, PET-CT or tissue sampling.
source: MacMahon H et al. Guidelines for Management of Incidental Pulmonary Nodules Detected on CT Images: Fleischner Society 2017. Radiology 2017

title: Lung mass
text: A lung mass larger than 30 mm carries a substantial probability of malignancy, particularly in smokers and older adults, and should be characterised with contrast-enhanced CT of the chest and upper abdomen and referred along a suspected lung cancer pathway.
source: NICE guideline NG122: Lung cancer - diagnosis and management

title: Atelectasis
text: Atelectasis is reduced lung volume. Direct signs are displacement of fissures and crowding of vessels and bronchi; indirect signs include raised hemidiaphragm, mediastinal shift towards the affected side and compensatory hyperinflation. Plate-like basal atelectasis is common after surgery and in poor inspiration.
source: Hansell DM et al. Fleischner Society Glossary. Radiology 2008; Radiopaedia: Atelectasis

title: Pulmonary oedema
text: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema progresses from upper lobe venous diversion to interstitial oedema (Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing) to alveolar oedema in a perihilar bat-wing distribution, often with cardiomegaly and bilateral effusions.
source: Gluecker T et al. Clinical and radiologic features of pulmonary edema. RadioGraphics 1999

title: Technical adequacy of a chest radiograph
text: Assess a chest radiograph for projection, rotation (spinous processes midway between the clavicular heads), inspiration (about six anterior or ten posterior ribs above the diaphragm), exposure (vertebrae just visible behind the heart) and coverage (apices and both costophrenic angles included). Inadequate films reduce sensitivity and can create false findings.
source: Royal College of Radiologists / standard radiographic teaching; Radiopaedia: Chest radiograph quality

title: Radiologist and AI together
text: Studies of chest radiograph AI as a second reader show that physician performance generally improves with AI assistance, but that incorrect AI suggestions can also mislead readers. Showing confidence and the evidence for each suggestion, and keeping the physician as the final decision maker, is recommended.
source: Seah JCY et al. Effect of a comprehensive deep-learning model on the accuracy of chest x-ray interpretation by radiologists. Lancet Digit Health 2021; Gaube S et al. Do as AI say. npj Digit Med 2021

title: Explanation type and physician trust
text: The type of AI explanation shown affects how physicians use advice: local explanations tied to the image region change diagnostic accuracy and confidence more than global explanations, and over-reliance is a risk when AI advice is wrong.
source: Prinster D et al. Care to Explain? AI Explanation Types Differentially Impact Chest Radiograph Diagnostic Performance and Physician Trust in AI. Radiology 2024

title: CheXpert
text: CheXpert is a dataset of 224,316 chest radiographs from 65,240 patients at Stanford, labelled for 14 observations with explicit uncertainty labels, widely used to train and benchmark chest radiograph classifiers.
source: Irvin J et al. CheXpert: A large chest radiograph dataset with uncertainty labels and expert comparison. AAAI 2019

title: Bias in chest X-ray AI
text: Chest radiograph classifiers can under-diagnose under-served subgroups, for example by sex, age, race or insurance status, even when overall accuracy is high. Subgroup performance should be monitored after deployment, not only at validation.
source: Seyyed-Kalantari L et al. Underdiagnosis bias of artificial intelligence algorithms applied to chest radiographs in under-served patient populations. Nat Med 2021

title: Calibration and uncertainty
text: Modern neural networks are often over-confident. Temperature scaling of the output logits is a simple, effective post-hoc calibration, and test-time augmentation gives a practical estimate of predictive uncertainty that can be used to defer uncertain cases to a human.
source: Guo C et al. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017; Ayhan MS, Berens P. Test-time data augmentation for estimation of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty in deep neural networks. MIDL 2018
